This refining margin equation is to illustrate that if we need refiners to have at least breakeven margins of zero to keep producing refined products, when freight cost goes up, cracks have to rise or crude FOB has to weaken.

There are of course other costs elements (e.g. utility costs for the refinery operations, working capital, vessel losses for the crude, etc).

Refinery yields can also be tweaked depending on the crude and refinery configuration but the biggest driver for the past month is the dirty freight cost.

The benchmark crude price (e.g. Brent) matters little in the refining margin equation because it cancels out with the product cracks which is the product price - crude benchmark. It only really factors into the operating cost element.

#oott

Refining margin = (Product yields * product cracks) - (crude benchmark + FOB premiums + freight cost)

The latest COT report on #commodities, covering the week to 20 October, showed net selling extending into a sixth consecutive week, during which the BCOM Index has fallen by 8%.

Once again, the bulk of the selling was concentrated in natural gas and metals, led by gold and, not least, copper. Grains also continued to attract selling, with the combined net long tumbling by 42% over the past four weeks after reaching an unsustainable record above 1 million contracts last month.

Across crude oil and refined products, demand was muted during a week of mixed price performance, with crude rallying while fuel products eased. The Brent net long 242k contracts was in line with the average seen during the past two months, and well below the 430k long recorded at the start of the Middle East disruption. 

In softs, all four contracts attracted net buying, led by coffee and sugar, with the latter's speculative net long reaching a fresh five-year high.

Speculative dollar longs remain near extremes – but where is the rally?

In the latest COT reporting week to 20 October, a 0.4% decline in the Bloomberg Dollar Index (BBDXY) helped trigger modest broad-based net dollar selling, particularly against GBP, JPY and CAD. The exceptions were AUD and NZD, which continued to attract selling.

Overall, the speculative gross dollar long was reduced by 11% to USD 40 billion but remains historically elevated. Despite this heavy positioning, the dollar has struggled to rally, raising questions about the strength of the underlying bullish conviction. Crowded positioning increases the risk of a sharp reversal should the macroeconomic outlook shift, potentially triggering an accelerated unwind of long dollar positions.

Key markets to watch: Crude oil, Treasury yields and AI-related equities. Together, they may determine whether the dollar finds support from ongoing inflation and risk aversion, or whether falling yields and an unwinding of crowded trades trigger a broader correction.

Commodity markets caught between risk-off sentiment and rising supply risks.

GEM NO. 2 (9735373) was attacked by Iran on 2026-10-09. The vessel had been anchored for an extended period with 2 million barrels of Saudi crude oil aboard and her AIS transponder switched on, making her an easy target. A fire broke out and was extinguished the same day. Satellite imagery captured the following day confirmed that the fire had been extinguished and showed no oil spillage in the water.
